title: UK Postcode Walking Route Planner
description: Plan a walking route between two UK postcodes with the UK Postcode Walking Route Planner — footpath routing, distance and time. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two London postcodes a mile apart as the crow flies can be a 1.4-mile walk once the Thames has chosen which bridge you will use.
quick_answer: The UK Postcode Walking Route Planner geocodes two UK postcodes and routes between them on footpaths and streets, with the walking distance and time. Type the start and destination postcodes, press plan, and follow the route on the map — the walk between any two British addresses, planned properly.
steps_intro: Britain runs on postcodes; walks should too. Two codes, one route:

body.t: Station to office, home to school: the walkable route with an honest time replaces the guessed one. General walking routes beyond postcodes live in the
“Ten minutes from the station” is a claim this page verifies — in routed minutes, not estate-agent minutes.
A prescribed 30-minute walk needs a route whose time is known before the door closes behind you.
Hotels give postcodes; walks start from them. The visitor's two codes become a route without local knowledge.
South-bank to north-bank postcodes route via the nearest bridge — the walk the map insists on, not the swim the straight line suggests.
A full UK postcode covers a handful of addresses on average, so the start point is usefully exact — the route begins at a real doorstep, not a district's middle.

popular_table.title: Walking times between postcodes
popular_table.intro: Orientation: routed walks run longer than crow distance, and time follows the pedestrian network. Your two codes give the real figures.
popular_table.note: Ranges are reading guidance for the planner's output, not measurements of your postcodes — bridges, cuttings and estates shape every real pair differently.

faq: Does the route use footpaths?
Yes — the pedestrian network: footpaths, streets and paths as the open data records them, which in Britain is a rich record.
Is the time realistic?
It is a routing estimate at walking speeds. Your own pace — measured by the Walking Pace Calculator — refines it; hills refine it further.
Does the route include live traffic?
No, and pedestrians are mercifully indifferent to most of it. Closures and works are the walker's version; the data snapshot is the limit.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Footpaths wind, bridges detour, estates gate. The planner's distance is the walkable one — the only one your feet will meet.
Can route results change over time?
New paths and corrected data change routes over seasons. Re-plan a standing walk occasionally.
Partial postcodes?
Full postcodes pinpoint best. A district code (SW1A) resolves to its middle — fine for area research, blunt for doorsteps.
Outside the UK?
This page is postcode-shaped for Britain. The Walking Route Planner takes any start and finish worldwide.
The route crosses private land.
Mapped paths can include permissive routes that close seasonally. Signs on the ground outrank the plan; divert and re-plan beyond the gate.
Walking time feels optimistic.
It assumes a steady adult pace on clear paths. Your Walking Pace figure, once measured, replaces the assumption.
Can I plan from a postcode to a place?
Postcode to postcode is the shape; for a named place as the other end, the Walking Route Planner takes free-form starts.
